name: Battleship Grey
lede: Battleship Grey is the flat, bluish-grey the US Navy painted its ships from the 1910s, made cheap and practical with barium sulphate, the same filler pigment that also went into First World War airplane camouflage paint.

sections.title: A paint built for a budget, not a mood
sections.body: Paterson's dictionary of color gives the plain, functional definition: the bluish-grey color in which battleships are often painted [1]. Ball supplies the chemistry behind the choice: barium sulphate, normally just a cheap white extender mixed into other pigments, became an important industrial paint ingredient in its own right because it was inexpensive, used both for First World War airplane camouflage colors and as a component of the US Navy's own Battleship Grey from the 1910s [2]. Garfield's survey of where color names come from sorts them into categories by what they are named after — geography, minerals, moods, mythology, and so on — and places Battleship Grey specifically under "end-use" names, colors named for the job they do rather than for a place, person, or material [3]. That is a tidy way to describe this color: it exists because a navy needed a cheap, unobtrusive grey, not because anyone was reaching for beauty.

sections.title: A red car wearing grey by accident
sections.body: St Clair tells a specific, almost comic case of the color's second life, far from any navy [4]. A historic car, now kept in Turin's Museo dell'Auto, is not the dashing red machine visitors expect, because it was once accidentally dropped into a dock in Genoa after a motor show [4]. To stop it rusting, it was repainted immediately with whatever paint could be found on hand: tins of battleship grey [4]. A once-red car has worn the navy's practical grey ever since, for no reason beyond what was sitting nearby.

sections.title: Its neighbors, and a nautical alias
sections.body: In the color graph, Battleship Grey sits 2.6 units from [[dusty-grey]], almost the same color, and 3.2 from [[middle-grey]], also almost indistinguishable [5]. [[pebble-grey]], 3.9 off, [[light-violet-grey]], 4.0 off, [[deep-gull-grey]], 4.4 off, and [[deep-plumbeous]], also 4.4 off, all read as close cousins rather than a different grey [5]. Among its own cross-system aliases is one that fits almost too neatly: Grey Boottopping, boottopping being the painted band along a ship's hull at the waterline — a nautical paint term landing, by name, on a nautical paint color [5].

sections.title: Seen in
sections.body: Among design aesthetics, the three closest full-palette matches are all within 2 units: Technicolor, 1.2 off, Surf, 1.4 off, and Science Academia, 1.8 off, all matched on this exact swatch [6]. On screen, a genuinely surprising match: Zhang Yimou's *Raise the Red Lantern*, a film built around saturated red, still carries a grey 2.3 units from this one somewhere in its palette, likely its courtyard stone and shadow [7]. Three garments land close by: a Qing-dynasty Chinese fragment, 0.7 units off; an American dress, 0.9 off; and a fifteenth-century Indian fragment, 1.0 off [8].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds this grey in 565 of 23,778 paintings, about 2.4 percent as photographed; a stricter within-painting lens finds it in 309 [9]. That makes it more common than 76 percent of the named colors in the archive [9]. Inside a painting it most often plays a mid-tone, 41 percent of its 309 clearest matches, by lightness rank within each canvas so an aged varnish cannot fake the result [9]. Its most devoted painter is Henri Matisse, carrying it in 6 of 50 works here, 4.6 times the predicted rate, and it shares canvases with Blackish Grey and Cool Grey far more than chance alone would explain [9].

It peaks century-wide and by single decade in the same place, the 1900s, 2.5 to 2.7 percent of the paintings we have from then, 1.7 to 1.8 times the expected rate [9]. The earliest match in the archive is from 1278, with 469 dated paintings carrying it through to 1937; the archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor, not a first, and a 1278 match sits 634 years before the name's own earliest record in our sources, 1912 [9]. In printed English the word itself peaks in the 1910s and rose fastest in the 1910s too, the exact decade the US Navy adopted the paint — one of the rare cases where the word's own print history and the practical history line up [9]. This is a computed color match on photographed, varnished canvases, not a pigment test.

questions.q: What cheap pigment made Battleship Grey practical for the US Navy to use fleet-wide from the 1910s?
Why does a historic car in Turin's Museo dell'Auto now look grey instead of its original red?
choices: It was repainted with whatever paint was on hand, battleship grey, after an accident
Red paint fades to grey over a century
The museum repainted it for a special exhibit
questions.answer: It was repainted with whatever paint was on hand, battleship grey, after an accident

questions.q: What does "boottopping," the nautical term behind one of Battleship Grey's aliases, actually refer to?
choices: The painted band along a ship's hull at the waterline
A type of naval uniform boot
questions.answer: The painted band along a ship's hull at the waterline

openers: A historic car in a Turin museum is grey today only because battleship-grey paint happened to be on hand after it was accidentally dropped into a dock.
This color's print history and its practical history agree almost exactly: the word peaked in the 1910s, the same decade the US Navy adopted the paint.
